node-1.label: A 51-year-old man presented with a 6-year history of chronic cough

node-2.label: Cough was productive with an egg cup full of sputum daily, present day and night, associated with numerous triggers, rated 9/10 in severity, occurred largely in bouts often with retching and dizziness, and worsened in severity over the previous 2 years; he denied haemoptysis or breathlessness and weight was stable

node-3.label: Past medical history included a 15-year history of ulcerative colitis, initially managed medically, with subsequent total colectomy in 2017 and re-anastomosis in 2018

node-4.label: He was an ex-smoker who quit in 1999, with a 5 pack-years smoking history, and worked in construction with occasional exposure to spray paints

node-5.label: Physical examination showed BMI 25 kg·m−2, no clubbing, and unremarkable chest examination

why.why: Both the laboratory physician and radiologist analyses reinforce that preserved FEV1/FVC with normal TLCO/KCO supports cough hypersensitivity as the leading diagnosis and argues against structural airway disease or significant COPD. The 6-year trigger-induced chronic cough with a normal chest examination and no red flags remains supportive. However, capsaicin cough reflex sensitivity and methacholine challenge were not performed, and laryngopharyngeal reflux and nasal examination data are absent, so cough-variant asthma, GERD, and upper airway cough cannot be fully excluded. Confidence therefore remains moderate at 0.55.

Both expert analyses note that laryngopharyngeal reflux and nasal examination data were not obtained, leaving GERD and upper airway cough inadequately excluded. This keeps GERD or upper airway cough as a plausible secondary consideration, but there are no direct reflux or nasal findings to raise confidence, so it remains at 0.25.

The radiologist explicitly interprets preserved FEV1, FVC, and normal TLCO/KCO as arguing against COPD despite a borderline FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.67, and the laboratory analysis also favours non-structural causes. Smoking and occupational spray-paint exposure provide only modest support for chronic bronchitis, so confidence is reduced from 0.12 to 0.08.

Both expert analyses agree that preserved spirometry with normal FEV1, FVC, and TLCO/KCO makes structural airway disease unlikely. A normal chest examination and absence of haemoptysis, breathlessness, and clubbing further refute significant structural airway pathology, so confidence is reduced to 0.03.

node-10.label: Spirometry shows FEV1 3.89 L (111% predicted), FVC 5.74 L (131% predicted), FEV1/FVC 0.67, and normal TLCO/KCO

node-11.label: Capsaicin cough reflex sensitivity was not performed

node-12.label: Methacholine bronchial challenge was not performed

node-13.label: Laryngopharyngeal reflux and nasal examination data were not obtained

why.why: The radiologist notes that FEV1/FVC 0.67 is borderline and that, without methacholine bronchial challenge, airway hyperresponsiveness cannot be excluded; the laboratory analysis also states that cough-variant asthma cannot be excluded. The chronic trigger-induced cough with bouts is compatible with cough-variant asthma, but preserved FEV1/FVC and normal TLCO/KCO keep confidence low, increasing only slightly from 0.10 to 0.15.

node-15.label: Cough hypersensitivity with cough-variant asthma component

why.why: The chronic, trigger-induced, bout-like cough is compatible with a cough-variant asthma component, and both experts highlight that methacholine challenge was not performed, so airway hyperresponsiveness remains possible. The borderline FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.67 adds a minor signal. However, normal FEV1, FVC, and TLCO/KCO prevent a higher confidence, so it increases from 0.30 to 0.35.

node-16.label: Cough hypersensitivity with laryngopharyngeal reflux component

why.why: Both expert analyses note that laryngopharyngeal reflux data were not obtained, so a reflux-related cough component cannot be excluded. This supports refining cough hypersensitivity to include a laryngopharyngeal reflux component, but without direct reflux testing confidence remains modest, increasing from 0.25 to 0.30.

node-17.label: Cough hypersensitivity with upper airway cough syndrome component

The absence of positive findings for asthma, reflux, or upper airway disease on available testing, combined with normal spirometry, a normal chest examination, and no red flags, supports an idiopathic/refractory cough hypersensitivity phenotype. Expert analyses do not provide new positive evidence for alternative causes, so confidence remains at 0.30 while confirmatory tests are still missing.
